executive_summary: August 2026 presents a striking split personality in investor sentiment. Both institutional and individual investors surged in their belief that the market would bounce back quickly from any sell-off — Buy-on-Dips confidence hit 100% among professionals and 87.5% among individuals. At the same time, crash anxiety actually increased, with fewer respondents confident that a crash won't happen. Investors seem to be saying: a sharp drop is plausible, but we'd buy right through it.

key_findings.headline: Pros Bounce Back, Individuals Steady
key_findings.interpretation: Institutional confidence in higher prices a year from now rebounded sharply to 85.71% after dipping to 66.67% in July. Individual confidence edged down to 72.22% from 80%, landing right where it was in June — this could reflect individual investors settling back to a baseline comfort level.

key_findings.headline: Crash Worries Hit New Highs
key_findings.interpretation: Only 30% of institutional investors and 22% of individuals feel confident a crash won't happen in the next six months — both readings dropped from July. In plain terms, most respondents now think a meaningful crash is at least plausible, even if not expected.

key_findings.headline: Universal Faith in Quick Recoveries
key_findings.interpretation: Every single institutional respondent in August said they believe a 3% single-day drop would fully recover within two days — up from 45.45% in July. Individual investors followed the same trajectory, jumping from 45.45% to 87.5%. This may suggest deep faith in market liquidity or simply a buy-the-dip reflex hardened by years of fast recoveries.

key_findings.headline: Valuation Views Diverge Again
key_findings.interpretation: Two-thirds of institutional investors now say the market is not overvalued, up from 60% in July, while individual investors held flat at 40%. Of course, some professionals subscribe to the view that in an efficient market the current price is by definition the right price, which may partially explain the institutional reading.

detailed_analysis:
The most eye-catching finding in August is the paradox between crash worry and dip-buying conviction. Think of it like a homeowner who buys extra fire insurance but also stocks the garage with lumber for renovations — they acknowledge the risk, yet they're ready to build the moment the smoke clears. Whether this reflects genuine analytical confidence or a behavioral habit formed during years of V-shaped recoveries is an open question.

Institutional investors had a volatile summer. Their 1-Year Confidence fell nearly 20 points in July before snapping all the way back in August. Meanwhile, their Buy-on-Dips reading went from 50% in June to 45% in July to a perfect 100% in August. Swings this large in a relatively small survey panel may partly reflect sampling variation, but they may also signal that professional sentiment is unusually reactive to incoming data right now.

Individual investors, by contrast, have been more stable on the 1-Year Outlook — hovering in the low 70s in both June and August with a brief pop in July. Their crash anxiety, however, has been consistently higher than the professionals'. Only about one in five wealthy individual investors feels confident a crash is very unlikely. One reading of this gap: individuals may weigh headline risks — geopolitical events, political uncertainty — more heavily than institutional managers who focus on earnings models and positioning.

The Valuation Confidence numbers deserve a footnote. At 66.67%, institutional investors are more comfortable with current prices than they were all summer. Individual investors remain skeptical at 40%. It's worth remembering that "overvalued" means different things to different people. For investors who believe markets are broadly efficient, the question itself is almost beside the point — price is simply where supply meets demand. For others, it's a warning flag. Both perspectives have long intellectual traditions behind them.
methodology: These indices come from the Yale/Shiller U.S. Stock Market Confidence Surveys, which have tracked investor sentiment since 1989. Each month, roughly 100 wealthy individual investors and 100 institutional investment managers answer the same standardized questions. The consistency of those questions over 35+ years is what makes the data meaningful — you can actually compare investor psychology across very different market environments. The four indices each measure something distinct: • 1-Year Confidence: The share who expect prices to be higher in 12 months. • Crash Confidence: The share who believe a crash in the next 6 months is very unlikely (under 10% probability). A low reading means most people think a crash is plausible. • Buy-on-Dips Confidence: The share who believe that after a 3% single-day market drop, prices would fully recover within two days. • Valuation Confidence: The share who do not believe the market is overvalued. Surveys were conducted semi-annually before 2001 and have been monthly since July 2001. Respondents rotate over time, but consistent characteristics — high income, investment experience — are maintained across the panel.
